li.a: War History Online: Le Paradis, the WW2 massacre of British soldiers which outraged even the Nazis
Neuengamme Concentration Camp Memorial: The Curiohaus Trials in Hamburg
BBC WW2 People's War: Le Paradis, the murder of 97 soldiers in a French field
Royal Anglian Regiment: The Le Paradis Memorial is dedicated in the presence of HRH The Princess Royal
Commonwealth War Graves Commission: Private George Ephraim Bromley
Roll of Honour: Massacre of Royal Norfolk soldiers at Le Paradis

content.p: On 27 May 1940, as the British army fell back towards Dunkirk, nearly a hundred men of the 2nd Battalion, Royal Norfolk Regiment, ran out of ammunition in a farm hamlet in northern France and gave themselves up. They were marched to a barn wall and shot with machine guns by men of the SS Totenkopf formation, and those who survived the guns were finished off with revolver shots and bayonets, according to the BBC archive. The BBC's wartime archive, the Commonwealth War Graves Commission and the regimental site Roll of Honour all give the number killed as 97. Two wounded men lived.

It took years for the story to be believed. One survivor was sent home in 1943 and was not listened to; the other spent the war in a prison camp. After 1945 their accounts, and the evidence of villagers, led investigators to Captain Fritz Knöchlein. A British military court in Hamburg found him guilty and sentenced him to death on 25 October 1948. He was hanged in January 1949, and War History Online describes him as the only man punished for the killings.
content.h2: A rearguard that was never meant to be rescued
content.p: The fighting that ended at Le Paradis belonged to the retreat to Dunkirk. War History Online says the German advance paused for three days, and that about 330,000 Allied troops had made it out of France by 4 June when the evacuation ended. Someone had to buy that time. The Royal Norfolks, together with the 8th Lancashire Fusiliers, were ordered to delay the Germans however long they could from three villages: Riez du Vinage, Le Cornet Malo and Le Paradis itself. The Royal Anglian Regiment's own account puts it bluntly: this was a rearguard that would fight to the last bullet, with no hope of evacuation.

Facing them was the SS Totenkopf, led by Theodor Eicke. War History Online describes it as a paramilitary force that took heavier casualties than other German units in the opening months of the war, and says the division had already been fired on while crossing the La Bassée river on 24 May, before being pulled back and sent across again two days later. On the morning of 27 May it attacked Le Cornet Malo; the same site counts some 150 dead on both sides and about 500 wounded there before the British surrendered.

The Norfolks' headquarters stood about a mile north of Le Paradis at Cornet Farm. At 11:30 a.m. they received what War History Online calls their last orders: do the best they could. They dug in around the farm and held on until they were driven from the ruined farmhouse into a nearby cowshed. The account of the fight quoted by the war graves commission places the surrender in the early afternoon, while War History Online says the ammunition ran out at about 5:15 p.m. By then, it says, 99 men remained under Major Lisle Ryder. The BBC archive and Roll of Honour say 97 surrendered, so the figures differ by two.

The commission's account, which it takes from a book by L. Aitken, says that two or three men who first came out waving a white towel were shot down. The rest, more than 90, then emerged, and the Germans accepted their surrender with cheers. Many of the prisoners were wounded, and the account says they were roughly handled with boots and rifle butts. The Germans were angry, the account says, because of their own heavy losses and the death of their battalion commander. War History Online names a Colonel Hans Friedemann Götze as the German officer facing the British and says he was killed during the fight at the farm.

The prisoners were paraded along the road and then marched into a paddock beside a large barn. As they entered, some saw two machine guns trained on the barn wall. The men were lined up along that wall and the guns opened fire, sweeping from left to right. Because of what the account calls the inefficiency of the gunners, many did not die at once and were killed with rifle and pistol fire and bayonets.

Some of the Royal Scots, a second British unit nearby, fared no better. They had surrendered at the same time, and War History Online says that in the confusion the two groups gave themselves up to different German units. It reports that mass graves found in 2007 showed that about 20 Scots who had surrendered to the wrong unit were killed. Some men escaped the fate of their comrades by luck. Private Robert Brown, a Norfolks signaller, surrendered to regular army troops, who took him away before the shooting began. Ernie Farrow, a Norfolks veteran, missed the massacre because he had been sent hours earlier to demolish a bridge, was wounded and captured there, and later escaped; Roll of Honour says he was the subject of a book by Cyril Jolly.

The responsibility of the SS officer in command is stated differently by different pages. War History Online says Knöchlein had the prisoners disarmed, lined them against the wall and ordered his men to bayonet survivors. The Gravestone site says he ordered two machine guns turned on the men and had the dead buried quickly along the barn wall. The BBC archive and Roll of Honour name the unit as No. 4 Company of the 1st Battalion, 2nd SS Totenkopf Regiment, whereas War History Online calls it the 14th Company; the sources do not reconcile this.

Later events inside Germany's own ranks are described only by War History Online. It says a journalist, Gunter d'Alquen, reported what he had seen the next day, believing the men had been tried. General Erich Hoepner, who commanded German troops in France, is said to have tried to have Eicke dismissed and failed, and other officers allegedly challenged Knöchlein to a duel, though nothing came of it.
content.h2: Two survivors and a farmer's wife
content.p: O'Callaghan was hit in the arm and knocked down, and another body fell across him; he lay still. When the Germans had gone he found that Pooley was alive too, though his leg was smashed. He dragged and carried Pooley into a ditch which, War History Online says, turned out to be a pigsty. They lived for three days on raw potatoes and water from puddles until Madame Duquenne-Creton and her son Victor found them. The family owned the farm and sheltered the men at risk to themselves. The commission's account calls her Madame Creton, the farmer's wife.

When the two men realised the family might be discovered, they gave themselves up. The Wehrmacht's 251st Infantry Division took them prisoner and, War History Online says, spared the Duquenne-Cretons. Pooley's leg was amputated in a hospital in Paris. O'Callaghan stayed in a German prison camp for the rest of the war. In 1943 Pooley was sent home because he was no longer a threat to Germany.

The dead were buried where they lay, by local people acting on German orders, according to the BBC archive. In 1942 the bodies were exhumed and moved into the churchyard at Le Paradis, now the war cemetery, along with casualties from scattered graves nearby. The commission says only about 50 of the 97 were identified, and the BBC page says nearly a third of the more than 150 casualties now commemorated there are unidentified. Private George Bromley of the 2nd Norfolks was among those identified, and the commission says he was reburied there between 1 and 15 May 1942. Another grave, inscribed for 19-year-old Private J. W. Raybould of the Royal Norfolk Regiment, carries a verse beginning, "Love will dream, and faith will trust".

Pooley told his story to the authorities at the Richmond Convalescent Camp, but War History Online says no one believed him. After the war he went back to Le Paradis in September 1946, and the local newspaper Nord Éclair interviewed him. Residents confirmed what he said, which the same site says angered the British authorities. Roll of Honour credits that visit with setting the wheels of justice in motion.

The task passed to the War Crimes Investigation Unit. Lieutenant Colonel A. P. Scotland wrote in his memoir, The London Cage, that he and his officers had spent two years on the inquiry. The Gravestone site, which quotes his book, says that the War Office added a notice distancing itself from the book's facts and opinions. Scotland wrote that one witness, an elderly French woman he named as Madame Romanie Castel, had never forgotten the face of the SS officer.

The pages disagree about where Knöchlein was found. The Gravestone site says he was eventually found in a prisoner-of-war camp in Sheffield, having been picked up by the Americans and interned in their camp in Yorkshire. War History Online says investigators found him living as a civilian and held him at the London District prisoner-of-war cage in Kensington Gardens. The Gravestone site adds that he later accused his interrogators there of torturing him, a claim that, according to War History Online, the court rejected.

Knöchlein was born in Munich on 27 May 1911 and joined the SS in 1934, the Gravestone site says, serving in the Totenkopf division under Eicke at a training area near Dachau. After France he commanded an anti-aircraft battery on the Russian front, rose to major in 1942, and in October 1943 took over a regiment of the 16th SS Panzer Grenadier Division. From March 1944 to January 1945 he led a Norwegian SS volunteer unit as a lieutenant colonel. He won the Iron Cross, the German Cross in Gold and the Knight's Cross. Scotland remembered him as "a Nazi of the first order", an opinion not a finding, but the nickname the site records for him is "the Butcher of Le Paradis".

His trial was one of 188 held by British military courts in the Curiohaus, a hall in Hamburg built for a teachers' association, which the British Army chose because bombs had not damaged it. The Neuengamme memorial explains that British courts tried only crimes against citizens of Allied countries. It gives the Knöchlein trial as running from 28 August to 25 October 1948, while other pages mention 25 October for the verdict. In Scotland's account of the hearing, on 12 October the elderly Madame Castel walked from the witness box towards the centre of the court, pointed at Knöchlein and cried: "That is him, that is the man!"

Knöchlein first denied being at Le Paradis, according to War History Online. When villagers identified him, he argued that the killings were justified because the British had used banned dum-dum bullets and had tricked his men with a white flag. The court did not accept any of it. At 3 p.m. on 25 October the president of the court announced a sentence of death by hanging, and the Gravestone site says that on hearing it Knöchlein turned grey but showed no other reaction. The same site says that, as it understands, his wife later tried unsuccessfully to have the conviction overturned.

He was hanged at Hameln at the age of 37. The executioner, Ted Roper, later remembered him as "very pompous and unrepentant to the end", and said that when asked his religion he snarled "atheist". The Neuengamme memorial gives the date of the hanging as 21 January 1949, while War History Online, the BBC archive, Roll of Honour and the Gravestone site say 28 January.

Angus Cain, 27, of the 1st Royal Scots, was reported missing believed killed after his hurried 1939 marriage in Hull. His widow only learned how he had died more than twenty years later, a relative wrote for the BBC archive, when she watched a 1960s television documentary about Pooley. Cyril Jolly's book about Pooley was published in 1956, according to Roll of Honour, which gives its title as The Revenge of Private Pooley.

Roll of Honour says a wall tablet was set into the barn in 1970. O'Callaghan wanted a more fitting memorial before he died, and Bill Priest, who had visited Le Paradis with him, was instrumental in building one near the church at Lestrem in 1978. Pooley died in 1982, and his ashes were buried in the war cemetery despite bureaucratic difficulty. A third memorial followed in 1991, and in 1994 local people placed a stone for the Royal Scots and Royal Norfolks beside the community centre.

No memorial stood in Britain until 2021. On 13 July that year HRH The Princess Royal attended the dedication of a monument outside Norwich Cathedral, a little more than two years after the project was proposed, the Royal Anglian Regiment reported. The regiment noted that about four memorials already existed in northern France, and that the cathedral would host larger services of commemoration, the first planned for 2022.
